course.title: Python for Beginners by Bro Code
course.description: Learn the fundamentals of Python programming in this highly interactive, beginner-friendly course. Perfect for those who have never written a line of code.
learning_outcomes: Set up your development environment and write your first Python program.
Understand and manipulate fundamental data types (integers, floats, strings, booleans).
Perform basic and complex mathematical operations.
Receive and process user input safely.
Control program flow using if/else statements and logical operators.
Automate repetitive tasks using while and for loops.
Store and manage collections of data using lists, sets, tuples, and dictionaries.

components.content: Hello World!
Welcome to Python! The very first thing any programmer learns is how to make the computer "speak." We do this using the `print()` function.

print("I like pizza!")
print("It's really good!")
Everything inside the quotes is called a "string" of text. You can use single quotes (' ') or double quotes (" ").
What is a Variable?
A variable is like a container or a box where you can store a value. It behaves exactly as the value that it contains.
Think of a variable as a labeled box. You can put a toy in the box and write "Favorite Toy" on the label. Whenever you need the toy, you just ask for the "Favorite Toy" box.

first_name = "Bro"
print(first_name)
Integers and Floats
In Python, there are different types of boxes for different types of data. Let's look at numbers.

# Integer (Whole number)
age = 21

# Float (Decimal number)
gpa = 3.2
You can perform math with these numeric variables directly.

age = age + 1
print("Your age is: " + str(age))
Text and Truth
A **String** is a series of characters (text). A **Boolean** represents True or False logic.

# String
name = "Bro"

# Boolean (Must be capitalized!)
is_online = True
if is_online:
    print("User is online")
else:
    print("User is offline")
The 4 basic data types: Int (whole numbers), Float (decimals), String (text), and Boolean (True/False).
Changing Data Types
Typecasting is the process of converting a value of one data type (integer, string, float, etc.) to another data type. Why do we need this? Because some operations only work on specific types.

name = "Bro"
age = 21
gpa = 3.2

# Convert a float to an integer (it drops the decimal)
gpa = int(gpa)
print(gpa) # Output: 3
You must cast numbers to strings before you can stick them onto another string.
print("I am " + str(age) + " years old")
Asking Questions
To make programs interactive, we use the `input()` function to ask the user a question.

name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello " + name)
`input()` ALWAYS returns a string. If you ask for their age and want to do math with it, you must cast it to an integer first!

age = int(input("How old are you? "))
age = age + 1
Basic Math
Python can act like a giant calculator.

friends = 5

friends = friends + 1
friends = friends - 2
friends = friends * 3
friends = friends / 2
friends = friends ** 2 # Exponent (Squared)
friends = friends % 2  # Modulo (Returns the remainder of division)
Built-in Math Tools
Python has built-in functions for common math operations.

pi = -3.14

print(abs(pi))    # Absolute value: 3.14
print(pow(pi, 2)) # Power: pi squared
print(round(pi))  # Rounds to nearest whole number
For more advanced math, you can import the `math` module.

import math

print(math.ceil(pi))  # Always rounds UP
print(math.floor(pi)) # Always rounds DOWN
Accessing Elements
Strings are sequences of characters. The indexing operator `[]` gives access to a sequence's elements.
Imagine a string as a train. Each letter is inside its own train car. Indexing is how we point to a specific train car. The tricky part? The first car is always car #0, not car #1.

name = "bro Code!"

first_char = name[0] # Returns 'b'
last_char = name[-1] # Returns '!'
Extracting Substrings
You can extract a slice of the string using the format `[start:stop:step]`.

name = "bro Code!"

first_name = name[0:3] # Returns 'bro'
last_name = name[4:]   # Returns 'Code!'
reversed_name = name[::-1] # A clever trick to reverse a string
Modifying Text
Strings come with built-in methods to manipulate them.

name = "bro code"

print(len(name))       # Length of string
print(name.find("c"))  # Finds first occurrence
print(name.capitalize()) # Capitalizes first letter
print(name.upper())    # Makes everything uppercase
print(name.replace("o", "a")) # Replaces all 'o's with 'a's
Cleaner Output
F-strings let you inject variables directly into a string, so you don't have to use typecasting and messy `+` signs.

name = "Bro"
age = 21

# The old, messy way:
print("My name is " + name + " and I am " + str(age))

# The clean, f-string way:
print(f"My name is {name} and I am {age}")
Branching Paths
An `if` statement executes a block of code only if its condition is true.
Multiple Conditions
You can add multiple conditions using `elif` (else if), and a catch-all block using `else`.
Order matters! The computer checks conditions from top to bottom. As soon as it finds a True condition, it skips the rest.
And, Or, Not
Logical operators are used to check if two or more conditional statements are true.
Repeating Blocks
A `while` loop executes a block of code as long as its condition remains true.

name = ""

while len(name) == 0:
    name = input("Enter your name: ")
    
print("Hello " + name)
This program will trap the user in a loop until they actually type something!
Loop Control Statements
You can change how a loop executes using `break`, `continue`, or `pass`.

while True: # Infinite loop!
    name = input("Enter your name: ")
    if name != "":
        break # Exits the loop entirely
Iterating Over Ranges
A `for` loop executes a block of code a limited amount of times.
Loops inside Loops
The "inner loop" will finish all of its iterations before finishing one iteration of the "outer loop".

rows = int(input("How many rows?: "))
columns = int(input("How many columns?: "))
symbol = input("Enter a symbol to use: ")

for i in range(rows):
    for j in range(columns):
        print(symbol, end="")
    print() # Moves to the next line
Multiple Items in One Variable
A list is used to store multiple items in a single variable. Lists are ordered and changeable.

food = ["pizza", "hamburger", "hotdog", "spaghetti"]
print(food[0])

food[0] = "sushi" # Updating an item
food.append("ice cream") # Adding an item
food.remove("hotdog") # Removing an item

for x in food:
    print(x)
Unordered, Unindexed Collections
A set is a collection which is unordered, unindexed, and does NOT allow duplicate values.
Unchangeable Collections
A tuple is a collection which is ordered and unchangeable. Once created, you cannot add or remove items.

student = ("Bro", 21, "male")

print(student.count("Bro"))
print(student.index("male"))

for x in student:
    print(x)
Key-Value Pairs
A dictionary is a changeable, unordered collection of unique key-value pairs. They are fast because they use hashing.
